stem: What is the main purpose of randomly assigning experimental units to treatments?
correct: It balances unmeasured background factors across the groups in expectation, so effects are attributable.
Unobserved factors balance out in expectation, so groups are comparable at the outset.

distractors.text: It guarantees the groups are exactly equal on every measured covariate in each single experiment.
distractors.misconception: confuses balance in expectation with exact balance

distractors.text: It increases the number of experimental units that are available for the analysis afterwards.
distractors.misconception: confuses randomisation with replication

distractors.text: It removes the need to measure covariates or to check the groups after the assignment.
distractors.misconception: treats randomisation as removing all diagnostics

distractors.text: It reduces the error variance by grouping similar units together before any treatment is given.
distractors.misconception: confuses randomisation with blocking

distractors.text: It ensures that the treatment effect is identical for every unit that takes part in the study.
distractors.misconception: confuses randomisation with homogeneous effects

explanation: Randomisation makes the assignment independent of every pre-treatment factor, measured or not, so groups are comparable on average. A particular randomisation can still be imbalanced by chance.

stem: A lab measures one sample of material ten times under the treatment and another sample ten times under the control. Why is it wrong to call this ten replicates per treatment?
correct: The ten readings share one experimental unit, so they are subsamples and not true replicates.
Replication needs separate experimental units, not repeated readings.

distractors.text: Ten readings is too few to estimate a variance, and at least thirty are always required per group.
distractors.misconception: invents a sample size rule

distractors.text: Repeated measurements are always more informative than extra units because they cut the noise further.
distractors.misconception: believes pseudo-replication is as good as replication

distractors.text: The two samples should have been measured on different days rather than one straight after the other.
distractors.misconception: focuses on timing, not on the unit

distractors.text: Replication matters only when the treatment effect is already known to be large in advance.
distractors.misconception: misunderstands the role of replication

distractors.text: Each reading should have been given its own block label instead of a control group being used.
distractors.misconception: confuses blocking with replication

explanation: The treatment was applied to one sample per arm, so the error estimate from repeated readings reflects measurement noise only. The comparison of treatments needs variability between independent units.

stem: When is blocking most worthwhile?
correct: When a known nuisance variable explains much of the response variation between comparable units.
When units form groups alike inside and different between.

distractors.text: When the units are already nearly identical, so that grouping them changes the error very little.
distractors.misconception: blocking pays off when units differ

distractors.text: When randomisation is impossible, because blocking can replace random assignment entirely in that case.
distractors.misconception: blocking does not replace randomisation

distractors.text: When the nuisance variable is itself changed by the treatment and is measured only afterwards.
distractors.misconception: post-treatment variables are not valid blocks

distractors.text: When the sample is so large that random variation is negligible and nothing needs to be done.
distractors.misconception: ignores that blocking targets nuisance variation

distractors.text: When there are more treatments than experimental units overall, so that groups must be formed.
distractors.misconception: confuses blocking with an incomplete design

explanation: Blocking removes variation due to the nuisance variable from the error term. It needs a blocking factor related to the response and fixed before treatment, and randomisation still takes place inside blocks.

stem: A website shows a new checkout page to all visitors in week 1 and the old page to all visitors in week 2, then compares conversion. What is the central flaw?
correct: Time and treatment vary together, so any change between weeks is mixed with the treatment effect.
The treatment is confounded with the calendar week, so their effects cannot be told apart.

distractors.text: Conversion is a binary outcome, which cannot be compared between two different calendar weeks.
distractors.misconception: wrong reason: binary outcomes can be compared

distractors.text: Two weeks is always too short a period to measure any difference in conversion rates.
distractors.misconception: invents a duration rule

distractors.text: Each visitor saw only one version, and between-visitor comparisons are never valid in any design.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a within-subject requirement

distractors.text: Using two periods doubles the type I error, since each week is tested separately against chance.
distractors.misconception: misdiagnoses the problem as multiplicity

distractors.text: Randomisation was used correctly, but the p-value was not adjusted for the number of visitors.
distractors.misconception: no randomisation was actually used

explanation: With no concurrent control, seasonality, campaigns or traffic mix cannot be separated from the new page. Assigning visitors at random to the two pages in the same weeks removes this.

stem: Which statement about the experimental unit is correct?
correct: It is the smallest entity independently given a treatment, setting the effective sample size.
The unit of randomisation decides the number of replicates.

distractors.text: It is the entity on which a measurement is taken, so more measurements per entity mean more replicates.
distractors.misconception: confuses the observational unit with the experimental unit

distractors.text: It is always a single person or animal, whatever way the treatments were actually assigned.
distractors.misconception: the unit depends on the assignment mechanism

distractors.text: It is chosen after the analysis as the level at which the treatment effect looks the largest.
distractors.misconception: data-driven choice of unit

distractors.text: It is the group of all units that carry the same block label in the design.
distractors.misconception: confuses the experimental unit with a block

distractors.text: It is whichever level has the largest variance, which then receives the most replication.
distractors.misconception: invents a rule

explanation: If treatments are assigned to whole classrooms, the classroom is the experimental unit, and the pupils inside are subsamples. Counting pupils as replicates overstates the information.

stem: Which assumptions underlie the one-way ANOVA $F$ test?
correct: Independent errors with mean zero and common variance across groups, approximately normal.
Independent, equal-variance, normal errors with mean zero within every treatment group.

distractors.text: Equal sample sizes in every group, which the $F$ test requires in order to be valid at all.
distractors.misconception: balance is not required

distractors.text: Normally distributed responses in the pooled sample, rather than within each treatment group.
distractors.misconception: the normality is of the errors within groups

distractors.text: Equal treatment means, since the test is built on the assumption that the null hypothesis holds.
distractors.misconception: confuses the null with the model assumptions

distractors.text: Errors that are positively correlated inside each group, which models the shared treatment.
distractors.misconception: independence is required

distractors.text: A linear trend in the group means across the ordered treatment levels.
distractors.misconception: confuses ANOVA with trend regression

explanation: The model is $y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\varepsilon_{ij}$ with $\varepsilon_{ij}$ i.i.d. $N(0,\sigma^2)$. Unequal group sizes are allowed.

stem: In a one-way ANOVA with $k$ groups and $N$ observations, what is the null distribution of $F=MS_{\text{between}}/MS_{\text{within}}$ under normal errors?
correct: An $F$ distribution with $k-1$ and $N-k$ degrees of freedom.
$F$ with $k-1$ numerator and $N-k$ error df.

distractors.text: An $F$ distribution with $k$ and $N$ degrees of freedom.
distractors.misconception: ignores the degrees of freedom used by the means

distractors.text: A $\chi^2$ distribution with $k-1$ degrees of freedom.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the within mean square is estimated

distractors.text: An $F$ distribution with $N-1$ and $k$ degrees of freedom.
distractors.misconception: swaps numerator and denominator degrees of freedom

distractors.text: A $t$ distribution with $N-k$ degrees of freedom.
distractors.misconception: confuses the F test with a t test

distractors.text: An $F$ distribution with $k-1$ and $N-1$ degrees of freedom.
distractors.misconception: uses total instead of error degrees of freedom

explanation: The between sum of squares has $k-1$ degrees of freedom and the within sum of squares has $N-k$. Their scaled ratio is $F_{k-1,N-k}$ under the null.

stem: In a balanced one-way design, what does the expected between-group mean square equal when the group means differ?
correct: It is $\sigma^2$ plus a positive term in the squared treatment effects, so $F$ tends to exceed 1.
It exceeds $\sigma^2$ by an amount growing with the spread of the group means.

distractors.text: It equals $\sigma^2$ whether or not the means differ, because both mean squares estimate the error variance.
distractors.misconception: true only under the null

distractors.text: It equals the within-group mean square exactly, in every sample that is drawn.
distractors.misconception: confuses expectation with sample equality

distractors.text: It is smaller than $\sigma^2$ when the means differ, because part of the variation is explained.
distractors.misconception: the explained variation adds to the between mean square

distractors.text: It equals the total variance of the responses taken without regard to the group labels.
distractors.misconception: mixes up between-group and total variance

distractors.text: It equals $\sigma^2$ divided by the number of groups $k$ whatever the treatment effects are.
distractors.misconception: invents a scaling

explanation: $E(MS_{\text{within}})=\sigma^2$ always, while $E(MS_{\text{between}})=\sigma^2+n\sum\tau_i^2/(k-1)$. The ratio exceeds 1 on average exactly when some $\tau_i\neq0$.

stem: After a significant ANOVA $F$ test, why are pairwise comparisons of the means adjusted (Tukey, Bonferroni)?
correct: Many pairwise tests at level $\alpha$ make some false positive likely, so familywise error needs control.
Unadjusted tests across all the pairs would exceed the intended familywise error rate.

distractors.text: The $F$ test is invalid once the data have been looked at, so the comparisons restore its validity.
distractors.misconception: the F test remains valid

distractors.text: Pairwise differences are not normally distributed even when the individual errors are normal.
distractors.misconception: differences of normal means are normal

distractors.text: Adjusting increases power so that smaller differences between pairs become easier to detect.
distractors.misconception: adjustment reduces power

distractors.text: The pairwise comparisons use variance estimates that cannot be pooled across the different groups.
distractors.misconception: the pooled within estimate is used

distractors.text: Adjustment guarantees that every pair that is declared different is truly different in the population.
distractors.misconception: confuses error control with certainty

explanation: With $k$ groups there are $k(k-1)/2$ pairs. Bonferroni uses $\alpha/m$ per test, and Tukey's method uses the studentised range to control the familywise rate.

stem: A one-way ANOVA $F$ test is not significant at 5%, yet the largest and smallest group means look far apart. What is the right caution?
correct: Choosing the extreme pair after the data is a selected comparison, so a naive $t$ test is too liberal.
The unadjusted p-value for the extreme pair overstates evidence.

distractors.text: A non-significant $F$ proves that all the group means are equal, so the extremes must be noise.
distractors.misconception: treats absence of evidence as evidence of absence

distractors.text: The $F$ test has no power at all against a difference confined to the two extreme groups.
distractors.misconception: the F test has some power against any difference

distractors.text: The extreme pair should be compared with a one-sided $t$ test, which recovers the lost power.
distractors.misconception: one-sided tests do not fix selection

distractors.text: Unequal group variances guarantee that the $F$ test fails to reject, whatever the data show.
distractors.misconception: unequal variances do not force non-rejection

distractors.text: Dropping the middle groups and rerunning the ANOVA on the extremes alone is a valid test.
distractors.misconception: data-driven subsetting invalidates the test

explanation: The range of $k$ means is larger than the difference of two pre-chosen means. A valid comparison of the extremes uses the studentised range or an adjusted procedure such as Tukey or Scheffe.

stem: In a $2^2$ factorial with factors $A$ and $B$, how is the main effect of $A$ defined?
correct: Mean response at high $A$ minus mean at low $A$, averaged over the levels of $B$.
The $A$ difference (high minus low) averaged over the two levels of $B$.

distractors.text: The $A$ difference measured at the low level of $B$ only, with the other cells ignored.
distractors.misconception: confuses a main effect with a simple effect

distractors.text: The change in the response when $A$ and $B$ are both raised from low to high together.
distractors.misconception: confuses main effect with a joint change

distractors.text: The difference between the two simple effects of $A$ at the two levels of $B$.
distractors.misconception: that is the interaction

distractors.text: The sum of the four cell means, divided by two, whatever the factor levels are.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a contrast that is not an effect

distractors.text: The $A$ difference at whichever level of $B$ gives the largest response.
distractors.misconception: cherry-picks the level of the other factor

explanation: Main effect of $A$ is $\tfrac12[(a b-b)+(a-(1))]$ in standard notation: the average of the two simple effects of $A$.

stem: A significant $AB$ interaction is found in a factorial experiment. What does this imply for the interpretation of the main effect of $A$?
correct: The effect of $A$ depends on the level of $B$, so the main effect alone can be misleading.
A factor's effect changes with the other, so check simple effects.

distractors.text: The main effects of $A$ and $B$ must both be exactly zero whenever there is an interaction.
distractors.misconception: interaction does not imply zero main effects

distractors.text: The factors $A$ and $B$ are correlated in the design, so their effects are confounded.
distractors.misconception: confuses interaction with confounding

distractors.text: The experiment was not randomised, so none of the effect estimates can be interpreted.
distractors.misconception: interaction is not a randomisation failure

distractors.text: The main effects are estimated with extra bias, so they should be discarded from the model.
distractors.misconception: main effects are still estimated without bias

distractors.text: One of the two factors can be dropped from the model without losing any information.
distractors.misconception: an interaction means both factors matter

explanation: The average effect of $A$ can hide opposite effects at the two levels of $B$ (a crossover). Report the simple effects of $A$ at each level of $B$.

stem: In a replicated $2^k$ factorial, why can every effect be estimated using all the runs?
correct: Each effect is a contrast of all the run totals with signs $\pm1$, and the sign columns are orthogonal.
Orthogonal sign columns let each effect use every run without confounding the others.

distractors.text: The effects are found one at a time, by holding the other factors at fixed levels in every run.
distractors.misconception: describes one-factor-at-a-time

distractors.text: Each effect uses only the runs where all the other factors are at their low level.
distractors.misconception: wastes the other runs

distractors.text: Using all the runs is possible only when no interactions exist among the factors.
distractors.misconception: interactions are estimated from the same runs

distractors.text: Each effect uses the variance from a single pair of runs, because the design is balanced.
distractors.misconception: invents a small effective sample

distractors.text: Pooling works only if the experiment is unreplicated, since replicates have different variances.
distractors.misconception: replication does not prevent the use of all runs

explanation: With $n$ replicates, an effect is the contrast divided by $n2^{k-1}$ and has variance $\sigma^2/(n2^{k-2})$. Each effect uses all $n2^k$ observations.

stem: Compared with varying one factor at a time, what is an advantage of a factorial design?
correct: It estimates interactions, and every run contributes to every main effect for the same budget.
Each run informs every main effect; interactions are estimable.

distractors.text: It needs more runs to estimate each main effect, in exchange for the ability to estimate interactions.
distractors.misconception: the factorial is more efficient, not less

distractors.text: It requires the interactions to be zero for its main effect estimates to be valid.
distractors.misconception: factorial estimates are valid with interactions present

distractors.text: It gives main effect estimates that are less precise, but avoids the multiplicity of testing.
distractors.misconception: the precision is higher

distractors.text: It can be analysed only when the number of factors is at most two.
distractors.misconception: factorials extend to any number of factors

distractors.text: It removes the error term, so no replication is needed to test the effects.
distractors.misconception: unreplicated designs lack a pure error estimate

explanation: In a $2^2$ design each main effect compares two runs against two runs, while one-factor-at-a-time estimates it from a single pair of runs. For the same budget the factorial is more precise and shows interactions.

stem: An unreplicated $2^3$ experiment has no pure error estimate. How can the effects be judged?
correct: Negligible effects look like noise about zero, so real ones leave the line on a normal plot.
Look for points off the line on a normal or half-normal plot.

distractors.text: Divide each effect by the grand mean and compare the ratio with a $t$ critical value.
distractors.misconception: the grand mean is not an error scale

distractors.text: Treat the three-factor interaction as the only valid error, since it is always exactly zero.
distractors.misconception: higher interactions are only often small

distractors.text: Use the largest effect as the error estimate for all the other effects.
distractors.misconception: the largest effect is the least like noise

distractors.text: Declare all effects significant, as there is no error to compare them with.
distractors.misconception: no error estimate does not mean significance

distractors.text: Compare each effect to the run-to-run variance within the single run of each cell.
distractors.misconception: a single run has no within-cell variance

explanation: With $2^3-1=7$ effects, if only a few are real, the rest estimate zero with common variance. They fall on a straight line on a normal plot.

stem: In a randomised complete block design, how are the treatments randomised?
correct: Separately inside each block, so every treatment appears once per block in random order.
Each block gets all treatments, allocated at random within that block.

distractors.text: Across the whole experiment at once, ignoring the block labels completely.
distractors.misconception: that would be a completely randomised design

distractors.text: Only between blocks, so that a whole block receives a single treatment.
distractors.misconception: confuses blocks with treatment groups

distractors.text: Not at all, because blocking already removes all differences between the units.
distractors.misconception: blocking does not remove the need to randomise

distractors.text: In the same fixed order in every block, to make the blocks easy to compare.
distractors.misconception: a fixed order confounds treatment with position

distractors.text: Within blocks, choosing in each block the treatment that looked best in a pilot run.
distractors.misconception: pilot-based choice is not random assignment

explanation: Randomising separately within each block protects against bias from unknown factors that vary inside blocks, while the block factor removes the known variation.

stem: Compared with a completely randomised analysis of the same data, what does the randomised block analysis change?
correct: Block variation is taken out of the error sum of squares, shrinking the error mean square.
Residual variance falls once block sums of squares are split out.

distractors.text: It increases the error degrees of freedom by the number of blocks that are used.
distractors.misconception: error degrees of freedom decrease by b-1

distractors.text: It removes treatment variation from the comparison instead of block variation.
distractors.misconception: swaps what is removed

distractors.text: It leaves the error untouched and doubles the treatment sum of squares.
distractors.misconception: invents an effect

distractors.text: It always improves the precision, even when the blocks are unrelated to the response.
distractors.misconception: ignores the cost in degrees of freedom

distractors.text: It replaces the $F$ test for treatments by a $t$ test on the block means.
distractors.misconception: the treatments are still tested with F

explanation: Fitting $b-1$ block parameters uses $b-1$ degrees of freedom. The gain is worth it only if block differences are large relative to $\sigma^2$.

stem: What defines a Latin square design with $p$ treatments?
correct: A $p\times p$ array with each treatment once in every row and column, blocking two nuisance factors.
Each treatment appears once per row and once per column of a $p\times p$ array.

distractors.text: Each treatment occurs once in every row, but the columns are chosen at random without a restriction.
distractors.misconception: ignores the column constraint

distractors.text: Each treatment occurs $p$ times in total, and the cells are filled at random.
distractors.misconception: ignores the row and column balance

distractors.text: Each row and column contains all treatments, and three nuisance factors are blocked at once.
distractors.misconception: a Latin square blocks two factors

distractors.text: Treatments are placed on the diagonal only, to separate the row and column effects.
distractors.misconception: invents a layout

distractors.text: Rows and columns are the treatments, and the cells hold the replicates of each pair.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a two-factor layout

explanation: The Latin square uses $p^2$ runs to compare $p$ treatments while removing row and column effects, a $p$-fold saving compared with the full crossing of the three factors.

stem: Which assumption is needed for the standard analysis of a Latin square?
correct: No interaction among rows, columns and treatments, so their effects simply add.
Additive row, column and treatment effects, with no interactions among them.

distractors.text: Equal row and column effects, so that the layout contributes no information at all.
distractors.misconception: confuses additivity with null blocks

distractors.text: Interactions between treatments and rows, which the square is constructed to estimate.
distractors.misconception: the square cannot estimate them

distractors.text: At least two replicates per cell, so that a pure error can be found within cells.
distractors.misconception: each cell has a single observation

distractors.text: Randomisation of the rows only, with the columns kept in their original order.
distractors.misconception: rows, columns and treatments are all randomised

distractors.text: A number of treatments greater than the number of rows in the layout.
distractors.misconception: squares have as many rows as treatments

explanation: Each cell has a single observation and the residual is formed from the leftover degrees of freedom, so interactions would inflate the error or bias the effects.

stem: Why can a small Latin square give weak tests of the treatment effect?
correct: Rows, columns and treatments use $3(p-1)$ of $p^2-1$ degrees of freedom, leaving $(p-1)(p-2)$ for error.
Few error degrees of freedom remain when $p$ is small, so the tests have little power.

distractors.text: It has more error degrees of freedom than a randomised block design, because two factors are removed.
distractors.misconception: removing factors reduces error degrees of freedom

distractors.text: Error has $p^2-1$ degrees of freedom because the three factors are not separately estimated.
distractors.misconception: ignores the fitted effects

distractors.text: The error degrees of freedom are zero by construction, so a Latin square needs replicates to test anything.
distractors.misconception: error df are positive once p is above 2

distractors.text: Error has $p-1$ degrees of freedom, the same number as each of the factors.
distractors.misconception: miscounts

distractors.text: The degrees of freedom do not matter, because the $F$ test is exact for any size of square.
distractors.misconception: ignores the critical value inflation at small df

explanation: For $p=3$ there are only $2$ error degrees of freedom, so the $F$ critical value is large. Replicating the square or using $p\ge5$ increases the power.

stem: Why use a $2^{k-p}$ fractional factorial design?
correct: To study many factors in few runs, assuming high-order interactions are negligible, with aliasing.
It saves runs by confounding some effects, trusting that high-order terms are small.

distractors.text: To estimate all the interactions exactly with fewer runs and no loss of information.
distractors.misconception: fractions always lose information

distractors.text: To increase the error degrees of freedom by adding replicate runs of the same settings.
distractors.misconception: a fraction does not replicate

distractors.text: To remove the need for randomisation, because the runs are chosen systematically.
distractors.misconception: the run order is still randomised

distractors.text: To make each main effect more precise than the full factorial gives with the same runs.
distractors.misconception: the precision is not improved

distractors.text: To avoid making any assumption about interactions, since all effects remain separately estimable.
distractors.misconception: the fraction relies on sparsity

explanation: A full $2^k$ needs $2^k$ runs. The fraction uses $2^{k-p}$ runs and relies on the sparsity of effects: high-order interactions are usually small.

stem: In a $2^{3-1}$ design with defining relation $I=ABC$, which effects are aliased?
correct: Each main effect with a two-factor interaction: $A$ with $BC$, $B$ with $AC$, $C$ with $AB$.
Each main effect is aliased with the complementary two-factor interaction.

distractors.text: Each main effect with the three-factor interaction itself, so that $A$ is aliased with $ABC$.
distractors.misconception: multiplies wrongly

distractors.text: Each main effect with another main effect: $A$ with $B$, $B$ with $C$ and $C$ with $A$.
distractors.misconception: main effects are not aliased with each other here

distractors.text: $A$ with $AC$, $B$ with $AB$ and $C$ with $BC$.
distractors.misconception: the alias is the product with the defining word

distractors.text: Only the two-factor interactions with each other, while all the main effects are clear.
distractors.misconception: main effects are aliased with interactions here

distractors.text: No effects are aliased, since all four runs have distinct sign patterns.
distractors.misconception: four runs cannot separate eight effects

explanation: Multiply an effect by the defining word and reduce squares to $I$: $A\cdot ABC=BC$. Four runs give four estimable contrasts, each the sum of two aliased effects.

stem: What does Resolution III mean for a fractional factorial?
correct: Main effects are clear of each other but aliased with some two-factor interactions.
Main effects are clear of each other but not of two-factor interactions.

distractors.text: Main effects are aliased with each other, but all the two-factor interactions are clear.
distractors.misconception: reverses the roles

distractors.text: Main effects are aliased only with interactions of three or more factors.
distractors.misconception: that is Resolution IV

distractors.text: Two-factor interactions are aliased neither with main effects nor with each other.
distractors.misconception: that is Resolution V

distractors.text: The design contains exactly three factors, each at two levels, in all of its runs.
distractors.misconception: confuses resolution with the number of factors

distractors.text: Each run of the design is replicated three times, so error can be estimated.
distractors.misconception: confuses resolution with replication

explanation: Resolution is the length of the shortest word in the defining relation. For Resolution III, main effects are aliased with two-factor interactions, and this is acceptable only if those interactions are small.

stem: How is the resolution of a fractional factorial read from its defining relation?
correct: It equals the number of letters in the shortest word of the defining relation.
The length of the shortest word in the defining relation.

distractors.text: It equals the number of words in the complete defining relation.
distractors.misconception: confuses with the number of generators

distractors.text: It equals the number of letters in the longest word of the defining relation.
distractors.misconception: uses the longest instead of the shortest word

distractors.text: It equals the number of factors $k$ minus the number of generators $p$.
distractors.misconception: confuses with the run size exponent

distractors.text: It equals the number of runs of the design, which is $2^{k-p}$.
distractors.misconception: confuses resolution with run size

distractors.text: It equals the number of effects that are aliased with each main effect.
distractors.misconception: confuses with the alias count

explanation: A word of length $r$ makes some effect of order $s$ aliased with effects of order $r-s$. The shortest word gives the lowest aliasing order, hence the resolution.

stem: A fractional factorial has Resolution IV. Which statement is true?
correct: Main effects are clear of two-factor interactions, but two-factor interactions alias one another.
Main effects are not aliased with any two-factor interaction in the design.

distractors.text: Main effects are aliased with two-factor interactions, while two-factor interactions are clear of each other.
distractors.misconception: reverses the roles

distractors.text: Every two-factor interaction is clear of all the other two-factor interactions.
distractors.misconception: this holds for Resolution V

distractors.text: Main effects are aliased with each other, though not with any interactions.
distractors.misconception: main effects are clear of each other in Resolution IV

distractors.text: All interactions up to order four are estimable separately from each other.
distractors.misconception: overstates what the design can resolve

distractors.text: Main effects are aliased with three-factor interactions, and also with some two-factor interactions.
distractors.misconception: contradicts the definition

explanation: The shortest word has length 4, so a main effect is aliased with three-factor interactions and a two-factor interaction with another two-factor one.

stem: In a standard A/B test of conversion rates, what does the null hypothesis state?
correct: The conversion rates under the treatment and control are equal, so the true lift is zero.
There is no difference in expected conversion between the two variants.

distractors.text: The treatment conversion rate exceeds the control rate by exactly the minimum detectable effect.
distractors.misconception: confuses the null with the design alternative

distractors.text: The observed rates are equal in the sample, with no sampling noise in the results.
distractors.misconception: confuses sample and population

distractors.text: The treatment is no better than the control with probability 95 percent.
distractors.misconception: treats the null as a probability statement

distractors.text: The p-value is at most the chosen significance level $\alpha$ in the experiment.
distractors.misconception: confuses the null with the rejection rule

distractors.text: The treatment effect is positive but too small to be of any practical interest.
distractors.misconception: confuses statistical and practical significance

explanation: $H_0:p_T=p_C$ is a statement about population rates. The data may or may not give evidence against it.

stem: What does a p-value of $0.03$ mean in an A/B test?
correct: With no real effect, results at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time.
Probability of a result at least this extreme if the null is true.

distractors.text: There is a 97% probability that the treatment really performs better than the control.
distractors.misconception: interprets the p-value as a posterior probability

distractors.text: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true, given the data.
distractors.misconception: the p-value is not the probability of the null

distractors.text: The treatment effect is 3% larger than the control effect in relative terms.
distractors.misconception: confuses p-value with effect size

distractors.text: Three percent of the users in the treatment arm were affected by the change.
distractors.misconception: confuses p-value with exposure

distractors.text: The test has 97% power to detect the observed effect at the chosen level.
distractors.misconception: confuses p-value with power

explanation: The p-value is $P(\text{data at least this extreme}\mid H_0)$. It is not $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$ and says nothing about the size of the effect.

stem: What makes a good primary metric (overall evaluation criterion) for an A/B test?
correct: It moves within the test duration and is aligned with the long-term goal of the business.
It is measurable, sensitive within the test period, and tied to the real goal.

distractors.text: It is the metric with the highest variance, so that effects are easiest to see.
distractors.misconception: high variance lowers sensitivity

distractors.text: It is whichever metric turns out to be significant, chosen after the experiment has run.
distractors.misconception: post hoc metric selection

distractors.text: It is a metric that the treatment can influence only indirectly, over several years.
distractors.misconception: too slow to be measured in a test

distractors.text: It is a guardrail metric that must stay unchanged, to show nothing has been harmed.
distractors.misconception: confuses the primary with a guardrail metric

distractors.text: It is the unweighted average of all the available metrics, so that none is left out.
distractors.misconception: dilutes the signal and the interpretation

explanation: The primary metric is fixed before the test. Guardrail metrics watch for harm, and proxy metrics must be validated against the long-term outcome.

stem: What does the randomisation unit determine in an online experiment?
correct: Which entity (user, session, device) is assigned as a whole, setting what counts as independent.
The entity that receives the same variant throughout, such as the user.

distractors.text: The fraction of traffic that is exposed to the new variant, between zero and one.
distractors.misconception: confuses the unit with the traffic share

distractors.text: The time window of the experiment, measured in a whole number of weeks.
distractors.misconception: confuses the unit with the duration

distractors.text: Only the denominator of the metric, and not the way the variants are assigned.
distractors.misconception: the unit governs assignment

distractors.text: The significance level used in the test, which is smaller for coarser units.
distractors.misconception: invents a link to alpha

distractors.text: Always the page view, because that choice produces the largest possible sample.
distractors.misconception: finer units cause interference between exposures

explanation: Randomising by user keeps each user's experience consistent. The analysis should then treat the user as the independent unit.

stem: Users are randomised, but click-through rate is computed as total clicks divided by total page views. What issue arises in a naive test treating page views as independent?
correct: Page views of one user are correlated, so the naive variance is too small and the test too liberal.
The analysis unit (page view) is finer than the randomisation unit (user).

distractors.text: Click-through rate cannot be tested at all, because it is a ratio of two counts.
distractors.misconception: the delta method handles ratios

distractors.text: Randomising users guarantees that every page view is an independent trial, so the test is valid.
distractors.misconception: page views within a user are dependent

distractors.text: The variance is overstated by the dependence, so that the test becomes too conservative.
distractors.misconception: the sign of the error is reversed

distractors.text: The test loses all validity because the randomisation unit was not the page view.
distractors.misconception: user-level randomisation is fine with a correct analysis

distractors.text: Heavy users make the ratio biased, which cannot be fixed by any variance formula.
distractors.misconception: the ratio is consistent; the variance is the issue

explanation: The correct variance clusters page views by user, for example by the delta method on user-level totals, or the analysis is done on a user-level metric.

stem: What is the statistical power of a test?
correct: The probability of rejecting the null when a specified nonzero true effect is present.
One minus the type II error rate at a specified nonzero effect size.

distractors.text: The probability that the null hypothesis is true when the test has rejected it.
distractors.misconception: confuses power with the false discovery proportion

distractors.text: The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when the true effect is exactly zero.
distractors.misconception: that is the type I error rate

distractors.text: The probability that the observed effect equals the true effect in the experiment.
distractors.misconception: confuses power with accuracy

distractors.text: One minus the significance level, whatever the size of the true effect.
distractors.misconception: confuses power with the confidence level

distractors.text: The probability that the confidence interval contains the true value of the effect.
distractors.misconception: confuses power with coverage

explanation: Power is $1-\beta$ and depends on the true effect, the variance, the sample size and $\alpha$. It is not one number for a test.

stem: What is the minimum detectable effect (MDE) in a power analysis?
correct: The smallest true effect that the test detects with the stated power at the chosen level.
The effect size at which power reaches the target, such as 80%, at level $\alpha$.

distractors.text: The smallest observed effect that would give a significant result in the collected sample.
distractors.misconception: confuses the MDE with the critical observed difference

distractors.text: The smallest effect of any business importance, whatever the sample size that is used.
distractors.misconception: confuses with the practical significance threshold

distractors.text: The expected effect of the treatment, as forecast by the product team beforehand.
distractors.misconception: confuses the MDE with a forecast

distractors.text: The standard error of the difference between the treatment and control means.
distractors.misconception: confuses the MDE with the standard error

distractors.text: The true effect at which the type I and type II error rates are equal.
distractors.misconception: invents a balance condition

explanation: The MDE is a design input chosen with the business, then used with $\alpha$, power and $\sigma$ to find the sample size. It is not an estimate from the data.

stem: How does the required sample size per group in a two-sample comparison depend on the effect size $\delta$ and the standard deviation $\sigma$?
correct: It grows like $\sigma^2/\delta^2$, so half the effect needs four times the sample.
The per-group sample size is proportional to $\sigma^2/\delta^2$ for fixed power.

distractors.text: It grows like $\sigma/\delta$, so halving the detectable effect needs about twice the sample.
distractors.misconception: forgets that variance is squared

distractors.text: It grows like $\delta^2/\sigma^2$, so a larger detectable effect needs more data.
distractors.misconception: inverts the dependence on the effect

distractors.text: It is independent of $\sigma$, once the power and the level are fixed.
distractors.misconception: ignores the noise level

distractors.text: It grows like $\sigma^2/\delta$, so halving the effect only doubles the sample.
distractors.misconception: the effect enters squared

distractors.text: It is proportional to $\delta$, so small effects need very few users.
distractors.misconception: small effects need more users

explanation: The standard error is $\sigma\sqrt{2/n}$. Requiring $\delta\approx(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})\sigma\sqrt{2/n}$ gives $n\propto\sigma^2/\delta^2$.

stem: With the sample size and true effect held fixed, which change increases the power of a two-sided $z$ test?
correct: Raising the significance level $\alpha$, at the cost of more false positives.
Accepting a larger type I error rate and so more false positives.

distractors.text: Lowering the significance level to make the test more stringent.
distractors.misconception: lower alpha lowers the power

distractors.text: Increasing the outcome variance by pooling in additional noisy metrics.
distractors.misconception: more noise lowers the power

distractors.text: Switching to a smaller true effect that is easier to model.
distractors.misconception: smaller effects are harder to detect

distractors.text: Using a two-sided rather than a one-sided test for the same alternative direction.
distractors.misconception: a two-sided test spends alpha on both tails

distractors.text: Stopping the experiment as soon as the first look gives a p-value below $\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: stopping rules change error rates, not power at fixed n

explanation: Power rises with a larger $\alpha$, a larger effect, a larger $n$ and a smaller $\sigma$. Each gain has a cost, apart from variance reduction.

stem: A test was powered for an MDE of 1% but the observed lift is 0.3% with $p=0.2$. What is the right reading?
correct: A non-significant result does not rule out a true lift below 1%, as power is low there.
Failing to reject says little about effects below the MDE.

distractors.text: It proves that the true lift is below 1%, so the treatment has no useful effect.
distractors.misconception: treats non-rejection as proof of no effect

distractors.text: The test must be rerun, since a p-value above $\alpha$ indicates a coding error.
distractors.misconception: non-rejection is a normal outcome

distractors.text: The sample can be extended until the p-value crosses 0.05 without affecting the error rates.
distractors.misconception: optional stopping inflates the type I error

distractors.text: The MDE should be reset to 0.3% and power recomputed afterwards to justify the null result.
distractors.misconception: post hoc power adds no information

distractors.text: Since the lift is positive, the result confirms that the treatment works at a lower level.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the evidence is weak

explanation: Absence of significance is not evidence of no effect. A confidence interval around 0.3% would likely include effects larger than 1% and zero.

stem: In a two-proportion $z$ test of $H_0:p_A=p_B$, why is a pooled proportion used in the standard error?
correct: Under $H_0$ the groups share one rate, so pooling best estimates the null variance.
The null says rates are equal, so one common rate is estimated.

distractors.text: Pooling makes the two samples independent of each other, which the test requires.
distractors.misconception: independence comes from the design

distractors.text: It is required because the two groups have the same sample size in the experiment.
distractors.misconception: pooling is not tied to equal sizes

distractors.text: The pooled estimate is unbiased for the difference in rates under any alternative.
distractors.misconception: it is built for the null only

distractors.text: It removes the need for a normal approximation when the counts are small.
distractors.misconception: the approximation is still used

distractors.text: Pooling lowers the variance whatever the truth, so it is also used for confidence intervals.
distractors.misconception: intervals use the unpooled variance

explanation: The test statistic uses $\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_A+1/n_B)$ with $\hat p$ pooled. A confidence interval for the difference uses the unpooled variance, because no null is assumed.

stem: With large samples in an A/B test of a mean metric, why is Welch's $t$ test usually preferred to the pooled-variance test?
correct: It needs no equal-variance assumption yet loses little power when variances are equal.
It stays valid when variances and sizes differ.

distractors.text: It assumes the metric is normal, which the pooled test does not need.
distractors.misconception: reverses the assumptions

distractors.text: It always has more power than the pooled test, whatever the true variances are.
distractors.misconception: it has less power when variances are equal and sizes unbalanced

distractors.text: It uses a smaller critical value, so its p-values are always smaller.
distractors.misconception: it is not simply more liberal

distractors.text: It compares medians, which are more stable than means for skewed metrics.
distractors.misconception: it compares means

distractors.text: It is exact for any sample size and any distribution of the metric.
distractors.misconception: it is approximate

explanation: Welch's statistic $(\bar x_A-\bar x_B)/\sqrt{s_A^2/n_A+s_B^2/n_B}$ has approximately a $t$ distribution with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

stem: Why can a $z$ or $t$ test be used for a skewed revenue-per-user metric in a large A/B test?
correct: The sample mean is near normal by the CLT despite skewed individual revenues.
Group averages are near normal whatever the user-level shape.

distractors.text: Skewness disappears once users are randomised, so the revenues become normal.
distractors.misconception: randomisation does not change the distribution

distractors.text: The test uses the median, which is normal for any data in a large sample.
distractors.misconception: the test uses the mean

distractors.text: The metric becomes normal once it is averaged over only a handful of users.
distractors.misconception: needs large samples, especially for heavy tails

distractors.text: Revenue is normal on the log scale, so the raw means are exactly normal.
distractors.misconception: confuses the log scale with the mean

distractors.text: The standard error is zero in large samples, so no distribution is needed.
distractors.misconception: the standard error shrinks but is not zero

explanation: The statistic is a sum of many independent terms. Very heavy tails make the approximation slow, so capping or transforming the metric can help.

stem: Why is the delta method used for a ratio metric such as clicks per page view?
correct: Both parts are random and correlated, so the ratio's variance needs linearising.
It gives the variance of a ratio of two sample means, allowing for covariance.

distractors.text: It turns the ratio into a proportion, so the binomial variance formula applies directly.
distractors.misconception: the ratio is not binomial

distractors.text: It makes the numerator and denominator independent, which removes the covariance term.
distractors.misconception: the covariance remains

distractors.text: It corrects the bias of the ratio to exactly zero in any sample size.
distractors.misconception: it is an approximation of the variance only

distractors.text: It is needed only when the denominator is a constant, such as the number of users.
distractors.misconception: it is needed when the denominator is random

distractors.text: It replaces the test with a permutation test applied to the numerator alone.
distractors.misconception: it is a variance approximation, not a permutation test

explanation: For $R=\bar X/\bar Y$, a Taylor expansion about $(\mu_X,\mu_Y)$ gives a linear function of $\bar X$ and $\bar Y$, whose variance includes their covariance.

stem: For $R=\bar X/\bar Y$ with $\mu_Y\neq0$, which terms enter the delta-method variance of $R$?
correct: Both mean variances and their covariance, scaled by the ratio and $1/\mu_Y^2$.
$\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)$, $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(\bar X,\bar Y)$, weighted by the ratio.

distractors.text: Only $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)$ divided by $\mu_Y$, since the denominator is treated as known.
distractors.misconception: ignores the randomness of the denominator

distractors.text: The sum $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)+\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)$ with no covariance term at all.
distractors.misconception: omits the covariance and the weights

distractors.text: The product $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)$ divided by the squared ratio.
distractors.misconception: invents a product formula

distractors.text: Only the covariance, since the variance of a ratio of means is otherwise zero.
distractors.misconception: the ratio has variance from both parts

distractors.text: The variances of both means, multiplied by $\mu_Y^2$ rather than divided by it.
distractors.misconception: gets the scaling of the derivative wrong

explanation: $\operatorname{Var}(R)\approx\frac{1}{\mu_Y^2}\left[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)-2R\operatorname{Cov}(\bar X,\bar Y)+R^2\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)\right]$.

stem: Why does checking an A/B test repeatedly and stopping at the first $p<0.05$ invalidate the test?
correct: Each look is another chance for a false positive, so the overall type I error rate exceeds 5%.
Each additional look adds another chance of a false positive under the null.

distractors.text: The p-value at each look is computed incorrectly from the partial data available then.
distractors.misconception: each p-value is valid at its own fixed sample size

distractors.text: Early looks have smaller samples, which turns the test into a one-sided test.
distractors.misconception: invents a mechanism

distractors.text: Looking changes the true effect, so the estimate is no longer measuring the same quantity.
distractors.misconception: looking does not change the effect

distractors.text: Early stopping is invalid only when the effect is large, and harmless otherwise.
distractors.misconception: the problem arises under the null

distractors.text: Checking is harmless provided the stopping time is written down only after the experiment.
distractors.misconception: a post hoc rule is exactly the problem

explanation: With many looks the probability of at least one $|z|>1.96$ under $H_0$ approaches 1. A fixed-sample p-value is valid only for a stopping time chosen in advance.

stem: What is an alpha-spending function?
correct: A rule setting the cumulative type I error allowed at each look, capped at $\alpha$.
It allocates the overall level $\alpha$ across the planned looks.

distractors.text: A function that raises the sample size at each look so that power stays at 80%.
distractors.misconception: confuses alpha spending with sample size re-estimation

distractors.text: A rule that spends the type II error budget as the experiment proceeds.
distractors.misconception: confuses alpha with beta

distractors.text: The p-value computed from all of the data collected up to the current look.
distractors.misconception: confuses the spending function with a p-value

distractors.text: A budget on the number of users who may be exposed to the new treatment.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a traffic limit

distractors.text: A penalty added to the test statistic after every look and removed at the end.
distractors.misconception: invents a mechanism

explanation: A spending function $\alpha^*(t)$ rises from 0 to $\alpha$ over information time $t\in[0,1]$. The boundaries at each look are chosen so that the cumulative rejection probability matches it.

stem: Compared with a fixed-sample $z$ test at $\alpha=0.05$ (critical value 1.96), how do O'Brien-Fleming boundaries behave across interim looks?
correct: Very strict at early looks, approaching the fixed-sample critical value near the end.
Large early critical values, shrinking to about 1.96 at the end.

distractors.text: They equal 1.96 at every look, since each interim look is a valid test on its own.
distractors.misconception: ignores the multiplicity of looks

distractors.text: They are lenient early and strict at the end, which favours stopping the experiment early.
distractors.misconception: reverses the shape

distractors.text: They stay constant across the looks at a value above 1.96, as in the Pocock rule.
distractors.misconception: describes Pocock boundaries

distractors.text: They start at zero and rise linearly up to the final look.
distractors.misconception: invents a shape

distractors.text: They fall below 1.96 at the final look, which compensates for the early looks.
distractors.misconception: the final boundary is slightly above 1.96

explanation: O'Brien-Fleming spends very little alpha early, so early stopping needs overwhelming evidence, and the final test is nearly as powerful as a fixed-sample test.

stem: What does an always-valid p-value or confidence sequence guarantee?
correct: Type I error control at any data-dependent stopping time, allowing continuous monitoring.
Validity under continuous peeking with arbitrary stopping.

distractors.text: Maximum power for a fixed sample size, so that experiments run shorter than needed.
distractors.misconception: confuses validity with efficiency

distractors.text: It removes the need for randomisation, since the stopping rule handles bias on its own.
distractors.misconception: randomisation is still required

distractors.text: Validity only at a pre-planned number of looks, and at no other times.
distractors.misconception: that describes group sequential designs

distractors.text: A p-value that can never exceed $\alpha$ once the null hypothesis is false.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a power statement

distractors.text: The same width as a fixed-sample interval, at no cost in precision.
distractors.misconception: ignores the price of continuous monitoring

explanation: Formally $P(\exists t: p_t\le\alpha)\le\alpha$ under $H_0$. Mixture sequential probability ratio tests give such p-values.

stem: What is the price of always-valid inference relative to a fixed-horizon test with the same data?
correct: Wider intervals, so less power at a given sample size, in return for freedom to stop at any time.
Intervals are wider and power is lower, in exchange for the freedom to stop anytime.

distractors.text: There is none, because the always-valid p-value equals the usual p-value at the final sample size.
distractors.misconception: the sequential p-value is larger

distractors.text: It requires the final sample size to be known before the experiment starts.
distractors.misconception: it does not require a fixed horizon

distractors.text: It inflates the type I error rate slightly, which is accepted for the sake of flexibility.
distractors.misconception: the type I error stays controlled

distractors.text: It can only be applied to binary metrics that have a fixed baseline rate.
distractors.misconception: it applies to means more generally

distractors.text: It needs the true effect size to be specified in advance, as in a power calculation.
distractors.misconception: always-valid methods need no effect size

explanation: Validity at all stopping times requires wider intervals at any given $n$. In practice it is the cost of being allowed to look at the results every day.

stem: What is the idea of CUPED?
correct: Subtract a multiple of a pre-experiment covariate from the outcome: unbiased effect, lower variance.
Regression adjustment using pre-experiment data to remove predictable noise.

distractors.text: Re-weight the users by their pre-experiment activity, so that heavy users count more.
distractors.misconception: weighting changes the estimand

distractors.text: Drop the users with unusual pre-experiment behaviour, which trims the outliers.
distractors.misconception: trimming is not CUPED and can bias the result

distractors.text: Increase the treatment fraction to 50% so that the two groups are of equal size.
distractors.misconception: confuses variance reduction with allocation

distractors.text: Replace the experimental metric by the pre-experiment outcome in the analysis.
distractors.misconception: the experimental metric is still the target

distractors.text: Adjust with a covariate measured after the treatment, since it explains most of the variation.
distractors.misconception: post-treatment covariates can bias the estimate

explanation: CUPED uses $Y-\theta(X-\bar X)$ with $X$ a pre-treatment covariate, usually the same metric from before the experiment. Randomisation keeps the adjustment unbiased.

stem: In CUPED with the optimal coefficient $\theta=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,X)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$, by what factor is the variance of the adjusted metric reduced?
correct: It is multiplied by $1-\rho^2$, where $\rho$ is the correlation of outcome and covariate.
By the factor $1-\rho^2$, with $\rho$ the correlation of outcome and covariate.

distractors.text: It is multiplied by $1-\rho$, so that the gain is linear in the correlation.
distractors.misconception: the reduction is quadratic in the correlation

distractors.text: It is multiplied by $\rho^2$, so a high correlation leaves only a small share of variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses the factor with its complement

distractors.text: It is multiplied by $1/(1+\rho^2)$, so it can never fall below one half.
distractors.misconception: invents a bound

distractors.text: It is multiplied by $1-\rho^2$ only for $\rho>0$, while a negative correlation raises it.
distractors.misconception: the sign of the correlation is irrelevant

distractors.text: It is divided by the ratio of the sample sizes in the two groups.
distractors.misconception: unrelated to the covariate

explanation: $\operatorname{Var}(Y-\theta X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)(1-\rho^2)$ at the optimal $\theta$. A correlation of $0.7$ removes about half of the variance.

stem: Why does CUPED not bias the estimated treatment effect?
correct: The covariate is measured before assignment, so it has the same mean in both arms.
Pre-treatment covariates are independent of assignment.

distractors.text: The coefficient $\theta$ is fitted separately in each arm so as to cancel any difference.
distractors.misconception: it is a single pooled coefficient

distractors.text: The adjustment cancels exactly in every sample, which makes the estimate noiseless.
distractors.misconception: the estimate still has sampling noise

distractors.text: The adjustment is applied to the control users only, leaving the treated users alone.
distractors.misconception: both arms are adjusted with the same $\theta$

distractors.text: The covariate is correlated with the treatment, so the adjustment absorbs the treatment effect.
distractors.misconception: a pre-treatment covariate is independent of assignment

distractors.text: Unbiasedness holds only if the covariate is a perfect predictor of the outcome.
distractors.misconception: any pre-treatment covariate works

explanation: $E[X]$ is the same in both arms, so subtracting $\theta(X-\bar X)$ has mean zero in the difference. A post-treatment covariate would break this.

stem: How does post-stratification (or stratified randomisation) reduce variance?
correct: Outcomes vary less within strata, so between-stratum variation is removed from the variance.
It removes the between-strata part of the variation from the estimate.

distractors.text: It increases the sample size inside each stratum by resampling the observed users.
distractors.misconception: resampling does not add information

distractors.text: It lowers the variance by discarding the strata that have the greatest spread.
distractors.misconception: discarding strata changes the estimand

distractors.text: It makes the treatment effect equal in every stratum of the population.
distractors.misconception: strata may have different effects

distractors.text: It helps only if the strata are unrelated to the outcome of interest.
distractors.misconception: strata must be related to the outcome

distractors.text: It shrinks the variance only if strata sizes are chosen after seeing the outcomes.
distractors.misconception: strata are defined before outcomes

explanation: The estimator averages stratum-wise differences with population weights, leaving only the within-stratum variance. Strata should be defined from pre-treatment variables correlated with the outcome.

stem: A covariate has zero correlation with the outcome. What happens if it is used in CUPED?
correct: The variance is not reduced, but the estimate stays unbiased.
No gain in precision, but no bias is introduced either.

distractors.text: The treatment effect estimate becomes biased toward zero.
distractors.misconception: adjustment with a pre-treatment covariate is unbiased

distractors.text: The variance of the estimate rises by a large factor.
distractors.misconception: the loss is tiny, from estimating the coefficient

distractors.text: The adjustment fails because the coefficient is undefined at zero correlation.
distractors.misconception: the coefficient is simply near zero

distractors.text: The variance is halved, as for any pre-period covariate.
distractors.misconception: the gain depends on the correlation

distractors.text: The type I error is inflated, because an extra parameter has been estimated.
distractors.misconception: the inflation is negligible for large samples

explanation: With $\rho=0$ the factor $1-\rho^2$ equals 1. The estimated $\theta$ is near zero, and the cost of estimating it is of order $1/n$.

stem: What is a sample ratio mismatch (SRM)?
correct: The observed split of users differs from the designed split by more than chance allows.
Arm sizes deviating significantly from the planned ratio.

distractors.text: A mismatch between the planned and the achieved effect size on the primary metric.
distractors.misconception: confuses with an effect size shortfall

distractors.text: A difference between the control and treatment means that is not statistically significant.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a null result

distractors.text: A mismatch between the sample size calculation and the actual length of the test.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a duration error

distractors.text: A situation where the treatment arm has a smaller variance than the control arm.
distractors.misconception: confuses with unequal variances

distractors.text: A change in the definition of the metric between the pre-period and the experiment.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a metric definition change

explanation: If a 50/50 split gives counts that a chi-square test rejects, users were lost or added in a way related to the assignment, which can bias the results.

stem: How is an SRM usually detected, and what should be done when it is found?
correct: Test arm counts against the design ratio with chi-square, then find the cause first.
Compare counts with the planned split, and find the cause before using the result.

distractors.text: Run a $t$ test of the metric between the arms, and if it is significant, accept the treatment.
distractors.misconception: SRM concerns counts, not the metric

distractors.text: Test the counts with chi-square, and if they differ, reweight the arms and proceed.
distractors.misconception: reweighting cannot repair the selection

distractors.text: Compare the counts by eye: a difference below 10% is fine and above 10% means an SRM.
distractors.misconception: invents a fixed threshold

distractors.text: Rerun the analysis with a smaller $\alpha$, since SRM disappears when the p-value is large.
distractors.misconception: misreads the diagnostic

distractors.text: Do a power calculation, since SRM is present whenever the power is below 80%.
distractors.misconception: confuses SRM with low power

explanation: A very small p-value of the chi-square test of the counts signals a problem in assignment, logging, or filtering. The effect estimate is unreliable until it is explained.

stem: What is a novelty effect in an A/B test?
correct: A temporary change in behaviour caused by a feature being new, which fades.
An early lift or drop from curiosity about the new feature that decays.

distractors.text: A lift that grows over the weeks as users learn how to use the feature.
distractors.misconception: that is a learning or primacy effect

distractors.text: An effect that appears only in new users and never in the existing ones.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a subgroup effect

distractors.text: Bias from assigning users to variants according to how new their accounts are.
distractors.misconception: confuses with non-random assignment

distractors.text: A treatment effect that is too small to be statistically detectable.
distractors.misconception: confuses with low power

distractors.text: The effect on the control arm caused by the presence of the treatment arm.
distractors.misconception: confuses with interference

explanation: Novelty makes early results overstate the lasting effect. Run the test long enough, and compare early and late cohorts or new and returning users.

stem: Why do social-network and marketplace experiments often violate SUTVA?
correct: A user's outcome can depend on others' treatment, such as neighbours or rival sellers.
Treated and control units spill over onto each other, contaminating the comparison.

distractors.text: Randomisation is impossible on networks, because the users are connected to each other.
distractors.misconception: randomisation is possible but the comparison is contaminated

distractors.text: Network users are always correlated with the covariates, so adjustment is needed to fix it.
distractors.misconception: the problem is interference, not covariates

distractors.text: The variance is infinite in networks, so that no estimate of the effect exists.
distractors.misconception: estimates exist but are biased

distractors.text: Only the treated users change their behaviour, while the control users never do.
distractors.misconception: control users are affected too

distractors.text: The bias disappears in large samples, by the law of large numbers.
distractors.misconception: more users do not remove the spillover

explanation: SUTVA requires each unit's outcome to depend only on its own treatment. With spillovers the difference in means estimates neither the global effect nor the direct effect.

stem: How can cluster or switchback randomisation help with interference?
correct: Whole clusters or periods are assigned together, so most spillover stays within a unit.
Assign clusters or periods, trading power for less spillover.

distractors.text: It randomises at a finer unit than the user to obtain more independent observations.
distractors.misconception: a finer unit increases the spillover

distractors.text: It keeps user-level randomisation and relies on a larger sample so that spillovers cancel.
distractors.misconception: spillover does not cancel with sample size

distractors.text: It removes the control group so that every user sees the treatment.
distractors.misconception: no comparison would remain

distractors.text: It uses a larger $\alpha$ to compensate for the bias caused by the spillovers.
distractors.misconception: alpha does not fix bias

distractors.text: It eliminates interference completely and costs nothing in statistical power.
distractors.misconception: there is always a cost in the number of effective units

explanation: Fewer, larger units mean fewer effective replicates and wider intervals. The gain is a smaller bias because the treated and control units interact less.
